```text
1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	\paragraph{Models.}
8	We evaluate on five architectures spanning different grouped-query attention (GQA) configurations:
9	\textbf{Qwen2.5-7B} (GQA ratio 7:1, 28 layers $\times$ 4 KV heads = 112 KV heads),
10	\textbf{Yi-1.5-9B} (8:1, 48 $\times$ 4 = 192 KV heads),
11	\textbf{Llama-3.1-8B} (4:1, 32 $\times$ 8 = 256 KV heads),
12	\textbf{Mistral-7B-v0.3} (4:1, 32 $\times$ 8 = 256 KV heads, sliding window attention),
13	and \textbf{Gemma-2-9B} (2:1, 42 $\times$ 8 = 336 KV heads, \texttt{head\_dim}=256, attention logit softcapping).
14	This selection spans GQA ratios from 2:1 to 8:1 and covers standard, sliding-window, and softcapped attention.
15	
16	\paragraph{Evaluation.}
17	We report perplexity (PPL, $\downarrow$) on the WikiText-2 test split (298{,}938 tokens) under bf16 inference with stride 512.
18	For downstream evaluation, we use ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, PIQA, and WinoGrande under 0-shot prompting.
19	
20	\paragraph{Profiling.}
21	Per-head sensitivity is measured by independently quantizing each head to each candidate bit-width in $\{2, 4, 8, 16\}$ and recording the PPL increase over the bf16 baseline.
22	We use two profiling resolutions: \emph{standard} (16 sequences $\times$ 512 tokens) and \emph{high-resolution} (64 sequences $\times$ 2048 tokens), both from WikiText-2 train.
23	Unless marked with $\dagger$, all results use standard-resolution profiling; Appendix~\ref{sec:profiling_resolution} analyzes the effect of resolution.
24	
25	\paragraph{Compression and constraint.}
26	The default target is 4$\times$ compression (average 4 bits, budget ratio 0.25).
27	The cardinality constraint limits 2-bit assignments to at most $k$ heads, where $k$ is selected via the compounding sweep described in \S\ref{sec:method} ($k{=}8$ for Qwen, $k{=}2$ for Yi-1.5 and Llama, $k{=}4$ for Mistral, $k{=}8$ for Gemma-2).
28	
29	\paragraph{Baselines.}
30	We compare against:
31	(1)~uniform 4-bit quantization;
32	(2)~unconstrained greedy allocation (RateQuant-style~\cite{zuo2026ratequant});
33	(3)~unconstrained MCKP allocation;
34	(4)~an L0-random heuristic that assigns Layer-0 heads to 8-bit and $k$ random non-Layer-0 heads to 2-bit, with remaining heads at 4-bit (5 seeds; we report mean$\pm$std and median);
35	and (5)~a naive positional heuristic that assigns Layer-0 to 8-bit and the $k$ deepest heads to 2-bit.
36	
37	\subsection{Main Results}
38	\label{sec:main_results}
39	
40	\begin{table}[t]
41	\centering
42	\small
43	\caption{PPL ($\downarrow$) on WikiText-2 at 4$\times$ compression. Unconstrained allocation fails catastrophically on $\{2,4,8,16\}$; our cardinality constraint restores performance. Best constrained result per model in \textbf{bold}. $^\dagger$Hires profiling (64 seq $\times$ 2048 tok); standard profiling does not improve over uniform on these architectures. $^\ddagger$Best $k$ from ablation ($k{=}4$). The $\pm$0.06 on Qwen reports std over 3 calibration seeds (hires profiling); bit distributions are identical across seeds.}
44	\label{tab:main_results}
45	\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
46	\toprule
47	Model & Baseline & Uniform & \multicolumn{2}{c}{Unconstrained} & Ours \\
48	 & (bf16) & (4-bit) & Greedy & MCKP & (Constr.) \\
49	\midrule
50	Qwen2.5-7B      & 9.81  & 15.45 & 32.45 & 36.92 & \textbf{11.23}$\pm$0.06 \\
51	Llama-3.1-8B    & 8.09  & 8.47  & ---   & ---   & \textbf{8.45}$^\dagger$ \\
52	Mistral-7B-v0.3 & 7.04  & 7.13  & ---   & ---   & 7.16$^{\dagger\ddagger}$ \\
53	Yi-1.5-9B$^\dagger$       & 7.02  & 7.22  & ---   & ---   & 7.22 \\
54	Gemma-2-9B      & 8.90  & 9.03  & ---   & ---   & 9.05 \\
55	\bottomrule
56	\end{tabular}
57	\end{table}
58	
59	Table~\ref{tab:main_results} summarizes the main results.
60	On Qwen2.5-7B, constrained MCKP achieves 11.23 PPL, a 27.3\% reduction over uniform 4-bit (15.45).
61	Higher-resolution profiling (64 seq $\times$ 2048 tok) further improves this to 10.91; we report the standard-profiling result here and analyze the effect of profiling resolution in Appendix~\ref{sec:profiling_resolution}.
62	Without the cardinality constraint, both greedy (32.45) and MCKP (36.92) perform \emph{worse} than uniform---a catastrophic failure caused by excessive 2-bit assignments that compound across layers.
63	The constraint eliminates this failure mode entirely.
64	Across 3 calibration seeds, constrained MCKP yields mean PPL 10.99$\pm$0.06 (std is 1.3\% of the uniform gap), with 90.2\% three-way allocation agreement, confirming profiling stability.
65	
66	On Llama-3.1-8B, the improvement is marginal: 8.45 vs.\ 8.47 (0.2\%).
67	The profiler finds low sensitivity heterogeneity across Llama's 256 KV heads, leaving little room for non-uniform allocation to improve over uniform.
68	
69	On Mistral-7B-v0.3, constrained MCKP (7.16, $k{=}4$) is slightly worse than uniform (7.13, $+$0.4\%).
70	This is a genuine negative result: the profiler reports near-zero sensitivity differences across heads, meaning the optimization has no reliable signal to exploit.
71	Mistral's sliding-window attention may contribute to this uniformity by limiting head-level variation in effective context length.
72	
73	On Yi-1.5-9B$^\dagger$, constrained MCKP ($k{=}2$) achieves 7.22 PPL, essentially identical to uniform 7.22 ($<$0.01\% difference).
74	Despite having the highest GQA ratio in our evaluation (8:1) and the highest concentration tested (0.71), Yi-1.5's sensitivity is dominated by a single extreme outlier (Layer-4 Head-3, $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$), a spike pattern that leaves no cross-bitwidth gradient for the solver to exploit.
75	
76	On Gemma-2-9B (GQA 2:1), constrained MCKP ($k{=}8$) achieves 9.05 PPL vs.\ uniform 9.03---a 0.3\% degradation.
77	Gemma-2 has the most uniform head sensitivity distribution across its 336 KV heads, consistent with its low GQA ratio and attention logit softcapping.
78	
79	Unconstrained results for Llama, Mistral, Yi-1.5, and Gemma-2 are omitted (---) as those experiments were conducted only on Qwen, where the failure mode is most pronounced.
80	Figure~\ref{fig:allocation} visualizes the bit-width allocation on Qwen, showing how constrained MCKP protects Layer-0 heads at 8-bit while selectively assigning only the 8 least-sensitive heads to 2-bit.
81	
82	\begin{figure}[t]
83	\centering
84	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig3_allocation_comparison.pdf}
85	\caption{Bit-width allocation on Qwen2.5-7B at 4$\times$ compression. Uniform assigns all heads to 4-bit. Constrained MCKP protects Layer-0 heads at 8-bit and assigns the 8 least-sensitive heads to 2-bit.}
86	\label{fig:allocation}
87	\end{figure}

      "content": "\\section{Experiments}\n\\label{sec:experiments}\n\n\\subsection{Experimental Setup}\n\\label{sec:setup}\n\n\\paragraph{Models.}\nWe evaluate on five architectures spanning different grouped-query attention (GQA) configurations:\n\\textbf{Qwen2.5-7B} (GQA ratio 7:1, 28 layers $\\times$ 4 KV heads = 112 KV heads),\n\\textbf{Yi-1.5-9B} (8:1, 48 $\\times$ 4 = 192 KV heads),\n\\textbf{Llama-3.1-8B} (4:1, 32 $\\times$ 8 = 256 KV heads),\n\\textbf{Mistral-7B-v0.3} (4:1, 32 $\\times$ 8 = 256 KV heads, sliding window attention),\nand \\textbf{Gemma-2-9B} (2:1, 42 $\\times$ 8 = 336 KV heads, \\texttt{head\\_dim}=256, attention logit softcapping).\nThis selection spans GQA ratios from 2:1 to 8:1 and covers standard, sliding-window, and softcapped attention.\n\n\\paragraph{Evaluation.}\nWe report perplexity (PPL, $\\downarrow$) on the WikiText-2 test split (298{,}938 tokens) under bf16 inference with stride 512.\nFor downstream evaluation, we use ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, PIQA, and WinoGrande under 0-shot prompting.\n\n\\paragraph{Profiling.}\nPer-head sensitivity is measured by independently quantizing each head to each candidate bit-width in $\\{2, 4, 8, 16\\}$ and recording the PPL increase over the bf16 baseline.\nWe use two profiling resolutions: \\emph{standard} (16 sequences $\\times$ 512 tokens) and \\emph{high-resolution} (64 sequences $\\times$ 2048 tokens), both from WikiText-2 train.\nUnless marked with $\\dagger$, all results use standard-resolution profiling; Appendix~\\ref{sec:profiling_resolution} analyzes the effect of resolution.\n\n\\paragraph{Compression and constraint.}\nThe default target is 4$\\times$ compression (average 4 bits, budget ratio 0.25).\nThe cardinality constraint limits 2-bit assignments to at most $k$ heads, where $k$ is selected via the compounding sweep described in \\S\\ref{sec:method} ($k{=}8$ for Qwen, $k{=}2$ for Yi-1.5 and Llama, $k{=}4$ for Mistral, $k{=}8$ for Gemma-2).\n\n\\paragraph{Baselines.}\nWe compare against:\n(1)~uniform 4-bit quantization;\n(2)~unconstrained greedy allocation (RateQuant-style~\\cite{zuo2026ratequant});\n(3)~unconstrained MCKP allocation;\n(4)~an L0-random heuristic that assigns Layer-0 heads to 8-bit and $k$ random non-Layer-0 heads to 2-bit, with remaining heads at 4-bit (5 seeds; we report mean$\\pm$std and median);\nand (5)~a naive positional heuristic that assigns Layer-0 to 8-bit and the $k$ deepest heads to 2-bit.\n\n\\subsection{Main Results}\n\\label{sec:main_results}\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{PPL ($\\downarrow$) on WikiText-2 at 4$\\times$ compression. Unconstrained allocation fails catastrophically on $\\{2,4,8,16\\}$; our cardinality constraint restores performance. Best constrained result per model in \\textbf{bold}. $^\\dagger$Hires profiling (64 seq $\\times$ 2048 tok); standard profiling does not improve over uniform on these architectures. $^\\ddagger$Best $k$ from ablation ($k{=}4$). The $\\pm$0.06 on Qwen reports std over 3 calibration seeds (hires profiling); bit distributions are identical across seeds.}\n\\label{tab:main_results}\n\\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}\n\\toprule\nModel & Baseline & Uniform & \\multicolumn{2}{c}{Unconstrained} & Ours \\\\\n & (bf16) & (4-bit) & Greedy & MCKP & (Constr.) \\\\\n\\midrule\nQwen2.5-7B      & 9.81  & 15.45 & 32.45 & 36.92 & \\textbf{11.23}$\\pm$0.06 \\\\\nLlama-3.1-8B    & 8.09  & 8.47  & ---   & ---   & \\textbf{8.45}$^\\dagger$ \\\\\nMistral-7B-v0.3 & 7.04  & 7.13  & ---   & ---   & 7.16$^{\\dagger\\ddagger}$ \\\\\nYi-1.5-9B$^\\dagger$       & 7.02  & 7.22  & ---   & ---   & 7.22 \\\\\nGemma-2-9B      & 8.90  & 9.03  & ---   & ---   & 9.05 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:main_results} summarizes the main results.\nOn Qwen2.5-7B, constrained MCKP achieves 11.23 PPL, a 27.3\\% reduction over uniform 4-bit (15.45).\nHigher-resolution profiling (64 seq $\\times$ 2048 tok) further improves this to 10.91; we report the standard-profiling result here and analyze the effect of profiling resolution in Appendix~\\ref{sec:profiling_resolution}.\nWithout the cardinality constraint, both greedy (32.45) and MCKP (36.92) perform \\emph{worse} than uniform---a catastrophic failure caused by excessive 2-bit assignments that compound across layers.\nThe constraint eliminates this failure mode entirely.\nAcross 3 calibration seeds, constrained MCKP yields mean PPL 10.99$\\pm$0.06 (std is 1.3\\% of the uniform gap), with 90.2\\% three-way allocation agreement, confirming profiling stability.\n\nOn Llama-3.1-8B, the improvement is marginal: 8.45 vs.\\ 8.47 (0.2\\%).\nThe profiler finds low sensitivity heterogeneity across Llama's 256 KV heads, leaving little room for non-uniform allocation to improve over uniform.\n\nOn Mistral-7B-v0.3, constrained MCKP (7.16, $k{=}4$) is slightly worse than uniform (7.13, $+$0.4\\%).\nThis is a genuine negative result: the profiler reports near-zero sensitivity differences across heads, meaning the optimization has no reliable signal to exploit.\nMistral's sliding-window attention may contribute to this uniformity by limiting head-level variation in effective context length.\n\nOn Yi-1.5-9B$^\\dagger$, constrained MCKP ($k{=}2$) achieves 7.22 PPL, essentially identical to uniform 7.22 ($<$0.01\\% difference).\nDespite having the highest GQA ratio in our evaluation (8:1) and the highest concentration tested (0.71), Yi-1.5's sensitivity is dominated by a single extreme outlier (Layer-4 Head-3, $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$), a spike pattern that leaves no cross-bitwidth gradient for the solver to exploit.\n\nOn Gemma-2-9B (GQA 2:1), constrained MCKP ($k{=}8$) achieves 9.05 PPL vs.\\ uniform 9.03---a 0.3\\% degradation.\nGemma-2 has the most uniform head sensitivity distribution across its 336 KV heads, consistent with its low GQA ratio and attention logit softcapping.\n\nUnconstrained results for Llama, Mistral, Yi-1.5, and Gemma-2 are omitted (---) as those experiments were conducted only on Qwen, where the failure mode is most pronounced.\nFigure~\\ref{fig:allocation} visualizes the bit-width allocation on Qwen, showing how constrained MCKP protects Layer-0 heads at 8-bit while selectively assigning only the 8 least-sensitive heads to 2-bit.\n\n\\begin{figure}[t]\n\\centering\n\\includegraphics[width=\\columnwidth]{figures/fig3_allocation_comparison.pdf}\n\\caption{Bit-width allocation on Qwen2.5-7B at 4$\\times$ compression. Uniform assigns all heads to 4-bit. Constrained MCKP protects Layer-0 heads at 8-bit and assigns the 8 least-sensitive heads to 2-bit.}\n\\label{fig:allocation}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsection{Budget Sweep}\n\\label{sec:budget_sweep}\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Effect of compression ratio on Qwen2.5-7B. Constrained MCKP provides meaningful gains at moderate-to-aggressive compression ($\\geq$4$\\times$). Standard-resolution profiling; hires results in Appendix~\\ref{sec:profiling_resolution}.}\n\\label{tab:budget_sweep}\n\\begin{tabular}{cccc}\n\\toprule\nCompression & Uniform PPL & Constr.\\ MCKP PPL & $\\Delta$ PPL \\\\\n\\midrule",

{"result":"{\"success\": true, \"data\": {\"path\": \"/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0509_2/projects/ratekv/paper_framing.md\", \"content\": \"# Paper Framing — ratekv\\n\\n## Target Venue\\n- Primary: EMNLP 2026 Main (ARR submission)\\n- Deadline: ARR May 25, 2026 (11 days from today 2026-05-14)\\n- Track: Efficient Methods for NLP\\n\\n## bf16 Consistency Resolution (2026-05-14)\\n\\n**已解决**：qwen_bf16_reeval 确认 bf16 ≈ fp16（baseline delta=0.0006, uniform delta=0.005）。compounding_sweep bf16 rerun 不需要。\\n\\n**eval pipeline 一致性**：exp_e 使用了不同的 eval 参数（baseline=8.82, MCKP=9.57），与主 pipeline（baseline=9.81）不一致。hires_mckp_reeval 用统一 pipeline 重测：MCKP hires bf16=10.9131。**论文使用统一 pipeline 数字**。\\n\\n| 指标 | 统一 pipeline (bf16) | exp_e pipeline (bf16) | fp16 (旧) |\\n|------|---------------------|----------------------|-----------|\\n| Baseline | **9.8106** | 8.819 | 9.81 |\\n| Uniform 4-bit | **15.4454** | — | 15.45 |\\n| MCKP hires (max_2bit=8) | **10.9131** | 9.569 | — |\\n| MCKP lowres (max_2bit=8) | ~11.23 | 11.345 | 11.23 |\\n\\n## Core Insight\\n\\nPer-head KV cache quantization sensitivity varies dramatically across architectures, and the effectiveness of non-uniform mixed-precision allocation is fundamentally determined by the degree of this heterogeneity. We provide both the analysis framework — characterizing when non-uniform quantization helps via per-head sensitivity concentration metrics — and a surprisingly simple method fix: a cardinality constraint (≤k heads at 2-bit) that prevents compounding effects from profiler non-additivity and reduces the search space sufficiently that solver choice becomes irrelevant (greedy and MCKP produce identical allocations).\\n\\n## Core Claims (3 条)\\n\\n1. **Head sensitivity heterogeneity is architecture-dependent and determined by sensitivity *distribution shape*, not GQA ratio alone**: Per-KV-head quantization sensitivity is extremely non-uniform within models, but the *degree* of heterogeneity — measured by Top-5% concentration — varies across architectures independently of GQA ratio. Critical counterexample: Yi-1.5-9B (GQA 8:1, highest in lineup) shows only 0.49 concentration and FAILS, while Qwen2.5-7B (GQA 7:1) shows 0.59-0.66 and succeeds (+27.3%). The difference is distribution shape: Qwen has a *cluster* of sensitive heads (Layer 0, 4 heads with 26× dominance — \\\"spread\\\" pattern), while Yi-1.5 has a single extreme outlier (L4H3, 34% of total delta — \\\"spike\\\" pattern). MCKP benefits from differentiated sensitivity across a group of heads, not from one outlier. GQA ratio contributes to (but does not determine) heterogeneity; the reliable predictor is Top-5% concentration.\\n\\n2. **Cardinality constraint is the primary intervention; profiling benefit is architecture-dependent**: On non-consecutive discrete bit-widths {2,4,8,16}, unconstrained allocation — whether by greedy (PPL 32.45) or MCKP (PPL 36.92) — produces catastrophic results because per-head independent profiling distortions compound non-additively when many heads are simultaneously assigned extreme quantization. A cardinality constraint (max_2bit≤k) is a simple and sufficient condition: it prevents compounding AND reduces the feasible set to a regime where solver choice is irrelevant — constrained greedy and constrained MCKP produce identical bit allocations and PPL (Δ=0.0000, both 11.2312). The profiling benefit beyond the constraint (hires vs lowres) is architecture-dependent: substantial on high-heterogeneity models (Qwen), marginal on low-heterogeneity ones. The optimal k is determinable via small-scale compounding effect test (plan_004).\\n\\n3. **Constrained allocation effectiveness scales with concentration, providing a practical diagnostic**: Constrained allocation achieves 27.3% PPL improvement (11.23 vs 15.45) on high-concentration architectures (Qwen, Top-5%=0.59-0.66) while matching or underperforming uniform on low-concentration ones (Yi-1.5 ≈0% at 0.71 hires, Gemma-2 -0.3% at 0.23, Mistral -0.4% at 0.22, Llama +0.2% at 0.34-0.59). The practical diagnostic Top-5% > 0.50 correctly classifies all 5 models tested (n=5, 5/5 accuracy): the sole model above threshold (Qwen) shows strong benefit; all four below show negative/marginal. Under aggressive compression (≥5×), constrained allocation prevents catastrophic collapse even on low-concentration models (Llama 5.3×: constrained PPL 57.60 vs uniform 2-bit 2644). This provides practitioners a simple, testable diagnostic for when to invest in mixed-precision KV cache quantization.\\n\\n## Story Spine\\n\\n- **Problem**: KV cache quantization typically applies uniform bit-width across all heads. Per-head mixed-precision allocation promises better quality-compression tradeoffs, but two fundamental questions remain unanswered: (1) *when* does non-uniform allocation actually help — i.e., under what architectural and compression conditions does the added complexity pay off? (2) *how* to make existing allocation algorithms (greedy, MCKP) work correctly on hardware-aligned discrete bit-widths {2,4,8,16} where they currently fail catastrophically?\\n\\n- **Existing approaches & gaps**: RateQuant (May 2026) provides R-D optimal per-head allocation via continuous closed-form (Theorem 2) and discrete greedy (Algorithm 1, optimal on consecutive integers {2,...,6} per Proposition 6). However, on hardware-aligned non-consecutive sets {2,4,8,16}, RateQuant's greedy produces PPL 32.45 (vs optimal ~11.23) — the polymatroid structure that guarantees greedy optimality breaks. Moreover, unconstrained MCKP fares even worse (PPL 36.92) due to compounding effects from profiler non-additivity. Critically, neither RateQuant nor ARKV addresses *when* non-uniform allocation is beneficial.\\n\\n- **Our framing**: We present a systematic study of per-head KV cache quantization sensitivity across architectures and identify a surprisingly simple fix for the failure of existing algorithms on hardware-aligned bit-widths: a cardinality constraint limiting the number of heads assigned to extreme quantization levels.       "result": "{\"success\": true, \"data\": {\"path\": \"/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0509_2/projects/ratekv/paper_framing.md\", \"content\": \"# Paper Framing — ratekv\\n\\n## Target Venue\\n- Primary: EMNLP 2026 Main (ARR submission)\\n- Deadline: ARR May 25, 2026 (11 days from today 2026-05-14)\\n- Track: Efficient Methods for NLP\\n\\n## bf16 Consistency Resolution (2026-05-14)\\n\\n**已解决**：qwen_bf16_reeval 确认 bf16 ≈ fp16（baseline delta=0.0006, uniform delta=0.005）。compounding_sweep bf16 rerun 不需要。\\n\\n**eval pipeline 一致性**：exp_e 使用了不同的 eval 参数（baseline=8.82, MCKP=9.57），与主 pipeline（baseline=9.81）不一致。hires_mckp_reeval 用统一 pipeline 重测：MCKP hires bf16=10.9131。**论文使用统一 pipeline 数字**。\\n\\n| 指标 | 统一 pipeline (bf16) | exp_e pipeline (bf16) | fp16 (旧) |\\n|------|---------------------|----------------------|-----------|\\n| Baseline | **9.8106** | 8.819 | 9.81 |\\n| Uniform 4-bit | **15.4454** | — | 15.45 |\\n| MCKP hires (max_2bit=8) | **10.9131** | 9.569 | — |\\n| MCKP lowres (max_2bit=8) | ~11.23 | 11.345 | 11.23 |\\n\\n## Core Insight\\n\\nPer-head KV cache quantization sensitivity varies dramatically across architectures, and the effectiveness of non-uniform mixed-precision allocation is fundamentally determined by the degree of this heterogeneity. We provide both the analysis framework — characterizing when non-uniform quantization helps via per-head sensitivity concentration metrics — and a surprisingly simple method fix: a cardinality constraint (≤k heads at 2-bit) that prevents compounding effects from profiler non-additivity and reduces the search space sufficiently that solver choice becomes irrelevant (greedy and MCKP produce identical allocations).\\n\\n## Core Claims (3 条)\\n\\n1. **Head sensitivity heterogeneity is architecture-dependent and determined by sensitivity *distribution shape*, not GQA ratio alone**: Per-KV-head quantization sensitivity is extremely non-uniform within models, but the *degree* of heterogeneity — measured by Top-5% concentration — varies across architectures independently of GQA ratio. Critical counterexample: Yi-1.5-9B (GQA 8:1, highest in lineup) shows only 0.49 concentration and FAILS, while Qwen2.5-7B (GQA 7:1) shows 0.59-0.66 and succeeds (+27.3%). The difference is distribution shape: Qwen has a *cluster* of sensitive heads (Layer 0, 4 heads with 26× dominance — \\\"spread\\\" pattern), while Yi-1.5 has a single extreme outlier (L4H3, 34% of total delta — \\\"spike\\\" pattern). MCKP benefits from differentiated sensitivity across a group of heads, not from one outlier. GQA ratio contributes to (but does not determine) heterogeneity; the reliable predictor is Top-5% concentration.\\n\\n2. **Cardinality constraint is the primary intervention; profiling benefit is architecture-dependent**: On non-consecutive discrete bit-widths {2,4,8,16}, unconstrained allocation — whether by greedy (PPL 32.45) or MCKP (PPL 36.92) — produces catastrophic results because per-head independent profiling distortions compound non-additively when many heads are simultaneously assigned extreme quantization. A cardinality constraint (max_2bit≤k) is a simple and sufficient condition: it prevents compounding AND reduces the feasible set to a regime where solver choice is irrelevant — constrained greedy and constrained MCKP produce identical bit allocations and PPL (Δ=0.0000, both 11.2312). The profiling benefit beyond the constraint (hires vs lowres) is architecture-dependent: substantial on high-heterogeneity models (Qwen), marginal on low-heterogeneity ones. The optimal k is determinable via small-scale compounding effect test (plan_004).\\n\\n3. **Constrained allocation effectiveness scales with concentration, providing a practical diagnostic**: Constrained allocation achieves 27.3% PPL improvement (11.23 vs 15.45) on high-concentration architectures (Qwen, Top-5%=0.59-0.66) while matching or underperforming uniform on low-concentration ones (Yi-1.5 ≈0% at 0.71 hires, Gemma-2 -0.3% at 0.23, Mistral -0.4% at 0.22, Llama +0.2% at 0.34-0.59). The practical diagnostic Top-5% > 0.50 correctly classifies all 5 models tested (n=5, 5/5 accuracy): the sole model above threshold (Qwen) shows strong benefit; all four below show negative/marginal. Under aggressive compression (≥5×), constrained allocation prevents catastrophic collapse even on low-concentration models (Llama 5.3×: constrained PPL 57.60 vs uniform 2-bit 2644). This provides practitioners a simple, testable diagnostic for when to invest in mixed-precision KV cache quantization.\\n\\n## Story Spine\\n\\n- **Problem**: KV cache quantization typically applies uniform bit-width across all heads. Per-head mixed-precision allocation promises better quality-compression tradeoffs, but two fundamental questions remain unanswered: (1) *when* does non-uniform allocation actually help — i.e., under what architectural and compression conditions does the added complexity pay off? (2) *how* to make existing allocation algorithms (greedy, MCKP) work correctly on hardware-aligned discrete bit-widths {2,4,8,16} where they currently fail catastrophically?\\n\\n- **Existing approaches & gaps**: RateQuant (May 2026) provides R-D optimal per-head allocation via continuous closed-form (Theorem 2) and discrete greedy (Algorithm 1, optimal on consecutive integers {2,...,6} per Proposition 6). However, on hardware-aligned non-consecutive sets {2,4,8,16}, RateQuant's greedy produces PPL 32.45 (vs optimal ~11.23) — the polymatroid structure that guarantees greedy optimality breaks. Moreover, unconstrained MCKP fares even worse (PPL 36.92) due to compounding effects from profiler non-additivity. Critically, neither RateQuant nor ARKV addresses *when* non-uniform allocation is beneficial.\\n\\n- **Our framing**: We present a systematic study of per-head KV cache quantization sensitivity across architectures and identify a surprisingly simple fix for the failure of existing algorithms on hardware-aligned bit-widths: a cardinality constraint limiting the number of heads assigned to extreme quantization levels. This single intervention (a) prevents compounding effects, (b) reduces the search space to where solver choice is irrelevant — greedy and MCKP produce identical optimal allocations, and (c) can be parameterized via a small-scale compounding test. Beyond the method, we establish that the benefit of non-uniform allocation is architecture-dependent and quantifiable via per-head sensitivity concentration, providing practitioners a diagnostic for when mixed-precision is worthwhile.\\n\\n- **Headline result template**: \\\"We show that a simple cardinality constraint (≤k heads at 2-bit) is a simple and sufficient condition for correct per-head KV cache quantization on hardware-aligned bit-widths {2,4,8,16}: without it, both greedy and MCKP fail catastrophically (PPL 32-37); with it, both produce identical near-optimal allocations (PPL 11.23). Standard k=4 puts 4 heads in 2-bit and 252 in 4-bit, while hires k=16 detects more heterogeneity and allocates 16 to 2-bit, 238 to 4-bit, and 2 to 16-bit — the extra 2-bit heads hurt performance. If we constrain hires to k=4, the allocation might collapse back to something similar to standard k=4, making 7.16 plausible but unverified.

This is a real inconsistency: Table 1 claims hires profiling for Mistral but the reported 7.16 traces back to standard profiling.

Now I'm noticing another layer to this: the caption references the best k from ablation (k=4), but that ablation was run with standard profiling, not hires. The optimal k under hires profiling hasn't actually been determined.

I'm also seeing something odd with the Llama results — both the hires pipeline and the standard heuristic k=2 approach are reporting the exact same PPL value of 8.4498, which feels like too much of a coincidence to ignore. istic_k2` might also use hires profiling. For Mistral, `mistral_heuristic_k4` gives 7.1648, which matches the standard profiling result, and there's no corresponding hires k=4 experiment to compare against. Though I should check if there are earlier Mistral experiments that might have used hires data, since `mistral_ppl_profiles_hires.json` has been around for a while.

Looking at the `mistral_k_ablation` results, the k16 value of 7.3106 matches exactly with `mistral_hires_constrained16_results.json`'s mckp_ppl_max2bit_16 of 7.3107, which means this ablation is using hires profiling data.

So the k_ablation sweeps k=4 through k=18 all with the same hires profiles, and since k4_ppl=7.1648 matches the Table 1 value of 7.16, that means the reported result is indeed from hires profiling. The `mistral_heuristic_k4` result also matches this same value, suggesting it's using the same profiling source.

Now I'm checking whether `mistral_k_ablation` actually uses hires or standard profiles by looking at the k=16 result of 7.3106, which matches the hires constrained result almost exactly (7.3107), strongly indicating hires profiling was used. But then I notice the `mistral_c4_cross_dataset` experiment with standard profiling also gives 7.1648 at k=4, which is the same as the hires result—so both profiling methods are yielding identical values for Mistral at k=4.

The reason both match is that with only 4 heads quantized to 2-bit, the allocation is stable across profiling resolutions since Mistral has low heterogeneity among its heads. This means the † annotation might not actually be incorrect, just that the provenance of which profiling method was used remains ambiguous.

So for Mistral, NEITHER standard nor hires improves over uniform! But the footnote says hires does improve? No — the footnote says the opposite: "standard profiling does not improve over uniform on these architectures." It doesn't claim hires improves. It just uses the hires result because it's more thorough.

For Llama, hires does improve (8.45 < 8.47). For Mistral, hires also doesn't improve (7.16 > 7.13). The paper reports both with $\dagger$ to show the best attempt with hires profiling, even though Mistral still doesn't improve.

The diagnostic itself has been upgraded from a simple threshold check to a joint concentration plus shape analysis, but paper_framing hasn't caught up to that sophistication yet.

Looking at the diagnostic framework claim, paper_framing says the simple "concentration > 0.50" rule correctly classifies all 5 models with perfect accuracy. That's the real separator between cases where MCKP helps and where it doesn't.

Let me verify this joint condition holds across all five architectures. Qwen passes both thresholds and shows the benefit. Yi-1.5 fails the second condition despite high concentration. Llama and Mistral both fail the concentration threshold, so they don't benefit. The joint diagnostic correctly identifies which models actually benefit from the approach. The new joint diagnostic achieves perfect accuracy while the old single-threshold approach misses Yi-1.5's lack of benefit, so the paper's methodology is sound but paper_framing.md is still referencing the outdated approach—I should flag this discrepancy in a separate report.
